claim: FOXM1 is a transcription factor that is an oncoprotein and a top biomarker of poor prognosis in human cancer.
source: The FOXM1 transcription factor is an oncoprotein and a top biomarker of poor prognosis in human cancer.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Overexpression and activation of FOXM1 is frequent in high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC).
source: Overexpression and activation of FOXM1 is frequent in high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC), the most common and lethal form of human ovarian cancer, and is linked to copy number gains at chromosome 12p13.33.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by references to prior studies.

claim: FOXM1 overexpression in HGSC is linked to copy number gains at chromosome 12p13.33.
source: Overexpression and activation of FOXM1 is frequent in high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC), the most common and lethal form of human ovarian cancer, and is linked to copy number gains at chromosome 12p13.33.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: FOXM1 is co-amplified and co-expressed with RHNO1.
source: We show that FOXM1 is co-amplified and co-expressed with RHNO1, a gene involved in the ATR-Chk1 signaling pathway that functions in the DNA replication stress response.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: RHNO1 is a gene involved in the ATR-Chk1 signaling pathway that functions in the DNA replication stress response.
source: We show that FOXM1 is co-amplified and co-expressed with RHNO1, a gene involved in the ATR-Chk1 signaling pathway that functions in the DNA replication stress response.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FOXM1 and RHNO1 are head-to-head (i.e., bidirectional) genes (BDG) regulated by a bidirectional promoter (BDP).
source: We demonstrate that FOXM1 and RHNO1 are head-to-head (i.e., bidirectional) genes (BDG) regulated by a bidirectional promoter (BDP) (named F/R-BDP).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: FOXM1 and RHNO1 each promote oncogenic phenotypes in HGSC cells, including clonogenic growth, DNA homologous recombination repair, and poly-ADP ribosylase inhibitor resistance.
source: FOXM1 and RHNO1 each promote oncogenic phenotypes in HGSC cells, including clonogenic growth, DNA homologous recombination repair, and poly-ADP ribosylase inhibitor resistance.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: FOXM1 and RHNO1 are one of the first examples of oncogenic BDG.
source: FOXM1 and RHNO1 are one of the first examples of oncogenic BDG, and therapeutic targeting of FOXM1/RHNO1 BDG is a potential therapeutic approach for ovarian and other cancers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is based on the novelty of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Therapeutic targeting of FOXM1/RHNO1 BDG is a potential therapeutic approach for ovarian and other cancers.
source: FOXM1 and RHNO1 are one of the first examples of oncogenic BDG, and therapeutic targeting of FOXM1/RHNO1 BDG is a potential therapeutic approach for ovarian and other cancers.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: FOXM1 promotes cancer by transactivating genes with oncogenic potential.
source: The forkhead/winged helix domain transcription factor FOXM1 promotes cancer by transactivating genes with oncogenic potential (Halasi and Gartel, 2013a; Kalathil et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cell phenotypes promoted by FOXM1 include cell cycle transitions.
source: Cell phenotypes promoted by FOXM1 include cell cycle transitions (Costa, 2005; Laoukili et al., 2005; Wonsey and Follettie, 2005), DNA repair (Maachani et al., 2016; Park et al., 2012; Monteiro et al., 2013; Khongkow et al., 2014; Roh et al., 2020), cell invasion and metastasis (Wang et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2019; Parashar et al., 2020), and chemoresistance (Roh et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2018; Tassi et al., 2017; Kwok et al., 2010; Carr et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cell phenotypes promoted by FOXM1 include DNA repair.
source: Cell phenotypes promoted by FOXM1 include cell cycle transitions (Costa, 2005; Laoukili et al., 2005; Wonsey and Follettie, 2005), DNA repair (Maachani et al., 2016; Park et al., 2012; Monteiro et al., 2013; Khongkow et al., 2014; Roh et al., 2020), cell invasion and metastasis (Wang et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2019; Parashar et al., 2020), and chemoresistance (Roh et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2018; Tassi et al., 2017; Kwok et al., 2010; Carr et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cell phenotypes promoted by FOXM1 include cell invasion and metastasis.
source: Cell phenotypes promoted by FOXM1 include cell cycle transitions (Costa, 2005; Laoukili et al., 2005; Wonsey and Follettie, 2005), DNA repair (Maachani et al., 2016; Park et al., 2012; Monteiro et al., 2013; Khongkow et al., 2014; Roh et al., 2020), cell invasion and metastasis (Wang et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2019; Parashar et al., 2020), and chemoresistance (Roh et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2018; Tassi et al., 2017; Kwok et al., 2010; Carr et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cell phenotypes promoted by FOXM1 include chemoresistance.
source: Cell phenotypes promoted by FOXM1 include cell cycle transitions (Costa, 2005; Laoukili et al., 2005; Wonsey and Follettie, 2005), DNA repair (Maachani et al., 2016; Park et al., 2012; Monteiro et al., 2013; Khongkow et al., 2014; Roh et al., 2020), cell invasion and metastasis (Wang et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2019; Parashar et al., 2020), and chemoresistance (Roh et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2018; Tassi et al., 2017; Kwok et al., 2010; Carr et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pan-cancer analyses have revealed that FOXM1 overexpression is widespread in human cancer and is linked to reduced patient survival and genomic instability.
source: Pan-cancer analyses have revealed that FOXM1 overexpression is widespread in human cancer and is linked to reduced patient survival and genomic instability (Jiang et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017a; Barger et al., 2019; Gentles et al., 2015; Carter et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There is high interest in FOXM1 as a cancer therapeutic target.
source: Accordingly, there is high interest in FOXM1 as a cancer therapeutic target (Tabatabaei Dakhili et al., 2019; Halasi and Gartel, 2013b; Gormally et al., 2014; Ziegler et al., 2019; Xiang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: High-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSC) is the most common and deadly subtype of epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC).
source: High-grade serous ovarian cancer, also known as high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC), is the most common and deadly subtype of epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) (Bowtell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Molecular features of HGSC include ubiquitous TP53 mutations, defects in DNA homologous recombination repair (HR), BRCA gene mutations, and robust genomic instability characterized by widespread copy number alterations (CNAs).
source: Molecular features of this tumor type include ubiquitous TP53 mutations, defects in DNA homologous recombination repair (HR), BRCA gene mutations, and robust genomic instability characterized by widespread copy number alterations (CNAs) (The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: FOXM1 pathway activation is a characteristic of >85% of HGSC cases and is linked to genomic instability.
source: Notably, FOXM1 pathway activation is a characteristic of >85% of HGSC cases and is linked to genomic instability (Barger et al., 2019; The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2011; Barger et al., 2015; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FOXM1 overexpression in HGSC and other cancers is driven by several mechanisms, including copy number gains, loss of function of p53 and pRB, activation of SP1, E2F1, and cyclin E1, and YAP signaling.
source: FOXM1 overexpression in HGSC and other cancers is driven by several mechanisms, including copy number gains, loss of function of p53 and pRB, activation of SP1, E2F1, and cyclin E1, and YAP signaling (Barger et al., 2019; Barger et al., 2015; Fan et al., 2015; Petrovic et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FOXM1 copy number gains in HGSC are localized to a region of chromosome 12p13.33 that contains 33 genes.
source: In particular, FOXM1 copy number gains in HGSC are localized to a region of chromosome 12p13.33 that contains 33 genes, and the FOXM1 CNA is functional, meaning that FOXM1 copy number directly correlates with FOXM1 mRNA expression (Barger et al., 2015; Song et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature and data in the manuscript.

claim: The FOXM1 CNA is functional, meaning that FOXM1 copy number directly correlates with FOXM1 mRNA expression.
source: In particular, FOXM1 copy number gains in HGSC are localized to a region of chromosome 12p13.33 that contains 33 genes, and the FOXM1 CNA is functional, meaning that FOXM1 copy number directly correlates with FOXM1 mRNA expression (Barger et al., 2015; Song et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature and data in the manuscript.

claim: It is highly plausible that other genes in the 12p13.33 amplicon contribute to HGSC, either independently or cooperatively with FOXM1.
source: It is highly plausible that other genes in this amplicon contribute to HGSC, either independently or cooperatively with FOXM1.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the context provided in the introduction.

claim: RHNO1 was initially reported to be overexpressed in a breast cancer cell line, localized to the nucleus, and promoted cell survival.
source: The initial report of RHNO1 (first called C12orf32) showed that it was overexpressed in a breast cancer cell line, localized to the nucleus, and promoted cell survival (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: RHNO1 was identified in a high-throughput screen for DNA damage response (DDR) regulators and was shown to physically interact with the RAD9, RAD1, HUS1 DNA clamp (9-1-1).
source: RHNO1 (reported as RHINO) was later identified in a high-throughput screen for DNA damage response (DDR) regulators and was shown to physically interact with the RAD9, RAD1, HUS1 DNA clamp (9-1-1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Through its interaction with 9-1-1 and TOPBP1, RHNO1 promotes the activation of ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related protein (ATR), a protein integral to the cellular DNA replication stress (RS) response.
source: Through its interaction with 9-1-1 and TOPBP1, RHNO1 promotes the activation of ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related protein (ATR), a protein integral to the cellular DNA replication stress (RS) response (Cotta-Ramusino et al., 2011; Lindsey-Boltz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The RHNO1 N-terminus contains a conserved APSES DNA binding domain, necessary for interaction with the 9-1-1 complex.
source: The RHNO1 N-terminus contains a conserved APSES DNA binding domain, necessary for interaction with the 9-1-1 complex, while the C-terminus is required for interaction with 9-1-1 and TOPBP1 and localization to sites of DNA damage (Cotta-Ramusino et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The RHNO1 C-terminus is required for interaction with 9-1-1 and TOPBP1 and localization to sites of DNA damage.
source: The RHNO1 N-terminus contains a conserved APSES DNA binding domain, necessary for interaction with the 9-1-1 complex, while the C-terminus is required for interaction with 9-1-1 and TOPBP1 and localization to sites of DNA damage (Cotta-Ramusino et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: X-ray crystallography was used to study the 9-1-1/RHNO1 interaction, and the data revealed that RHNO1 specifically interacts with RAD1.
source: Recently, X-ray crystallography was used to study the 9-1-1/RHNO1 interaction, and the data revealed that RHNO1 specifically interacts with RAD1 (Hara et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The expression, regulation, and function of RHNO1 in normal tissues and cancer are largely unknown.
source: The expression, regulation, and function of RHNO1 in normal tissues and cancer are largely unknown, but RHNO1 was recently identified as a hub gene associated with poor prognosis in colorectal cancer (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: RHNO1 was recently identified as a hub gene associated with poor prognosis in colorectal cancer.
source: The expression, regulation, and function of RHNO1 in normal tissues and cancer are largely unknown, but RHNO1 was recently identified as a hub gene associated with poor prognosis in colorectal cancer (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The prominence of the RS response in cancer cell survival and its recent emergence as a therapeutic target make investigation of the function of RHNO1 in cancer an important area of study.
source: The prominence of the RS response in cancer cell survival and its recent emergence as a therapeutic target make investigation of the function of RHNO1 in cancer an important area of study (Ubhi and Brown, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The ubiquity of elevated RS in HGSC makes this tumor type particularly relevant for RHNO1 investigation.
source: Moreover, the ubiquity of elevated RS in HGSC makes this tumor type particularly relevant for RHNO1 investigation (Konstantinopoulos et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: FOXM1 and RHNO1 are tightly co-expressed in both normal and cancer cells and tissues, including individual cells.
source: We show that FOXM1 and RHNO1 are tightly co-expressed in both normal and cancer cells and tissues, including individual cells, and that their co-expression is controlled by a bidirectional promoter (F/R-BDP).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: FOXM1 and RHNO1 co-expression is controlled by a bidirectional promoter (F/R-BDP).
source: We show that FOXM1 and RHNO1 are tightly co-expressed in both normal and cancer cells and tissues, including individual cells, and that their co-expression is controlled by a bidirectional promoter (F/R-BDP).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: FOXM1 is located at chromosome 12p13.33, a region showing frequent copy number gains in HGSC.
source: FOXM1 is located at chromosome 12p13.33, a region showing frequent copy number gains in HGSC, and amplification at this locus is associated with reduced patient survival (Barger et al., 2019; Barger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Amplification at the 12p13.33 locus is associated with reduced patient survival.
source: FOXM1 is located at chromosome 12p13.33, a region showing frequent copy number gains in HGSC, and amplification at this locus is associated with reduced patient survival (Barger et al., 2019; Barger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 12p13.33 amplification is detected from cell-free DNA in the plasma of HGSC patients at diagnosis and is further enriched in patients experiencing disease relapse.
source: Moreover, a recent study demonstrated that 12p13.33 amplification is detected from cell-free DNA in the plasma of HGSC patients at diagnosis and is further enriched in patients experiencing disease relapse (Paracchini et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The minimal 12p13.33 amplicon contains FOXM1 and 32 additional genes.
source: The minimal amplicon contains FOXM1 and 32 additional genes (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1.

claim: Among all amplicon genes, FOXM1 expression shows the strongest correlation with RHNO1 in TCGA HGSC data.
source: Using The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) data, we found that, among all amplicon genes, FOXM1 expression shows the strongest correlation with RHNO1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: FOXM1 and RHNO1 are located next to each other and arranged 'head-to-head', that is, they are BDGs.
source: Intriguingly, genomic analyses revealed that FOXM1 and RHNO1 are located next to each other and arranged 'head-to-head', that is, they are BDGs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Greater than 10% of human genes are bidirectional.
source: Greater than 10% of human genes are bidirectional, and the paired genes may be regulated by a bidirectional promoter (BDP) and have related functions (Trinklein et al., 2004; Wakano et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2007; Tu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Bidirectional genes may be regulated by a bidirectional promoter (BDP) and have related functions.
source: Greater than 10% of human genes are bidirectional, and the paired genes may be regulated by a bidirectional promoter (BDP) and have related functions (Trinklein et al., 2004; Wakano et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2007; Tu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cancer-related genes were recently shown to be highly enriched for BDG.
source: Furthermore, cancer-related genes were recently shown to be highly enriched for BDG (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Despite their strikingly high prevalence in the human genome and significant enrichment in cancer genes, the functional role of BDG has been infrequently studied.
source: Despite their strikingly high prevalence in the human genome and significant enrichment in cancer genes, the functional role of BDG has been infrequently studied (Chen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2015; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The F/R-BDP contained a CpG island (CGI), a common feature of BDP.
source: The F/R-BDP contained a CpG island (CGI), a common feature of BDP (Figure 2B; Wakano et al., 2012; Takai and Jones, 2004; Antequera, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2B and citations to prior literature.

claim: The F/R-BDP is fully hypomethylated in both normal and cancer tissues, including normal ovary (NO) and ovarian cancer.
source: Although differential DNA methylation of CGIs contained within BDP can regulate BDG expression (Shu et al., 2006), we found that the F/R-BDP is fully hypomethylated in both normal and cancer tissues, including normal ovary (NO) and ovarian cancer, suggesting that differential DNA methylation is not a regulatory mechanism at this BDP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differential DNA methylation is not a regulatory mechanism at the F/R-BDP.
source: Although differential DNA methylation of CGIs contained within BDP can regulate BDG expression (Shu et al., 2006), we found that the F/R-BDP is fully hypomethylated in both normal and cancer tissues, including normal ovary (NO) and ovarian cancer, suggesting that differential DNA methylation is not a regulatory mechanism at this BDP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ENCODE data revealed the presence of bimodal peaks of transcriptionally active histone modifications at the F/R-BDP, strongly suggestive of bidirectional transcriptional activity.
source: In addition to a CGI, BDPs are often enriched with specific histone marks (Bornelöv et al., 2015), and The Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) data revealed the presence of bimodal peaks of transcriptionally active histone modifications at the F/R-BDP, strongly suggestive of bidirectional transcriptional activity (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2B and a citation to prior literature.

claim: The F/R-BDP was characterized by DNase I hypersensitivity, enriched TF binding, active chromatin segmentation, and vertebrate conservation.
source: Additionally, the F/R-BDP was characterized by DNase I hypersensitivity, enriched TF binding, active chromatin segmentation, and vertebrate conservation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Among TF binding sites in the F/R-BDP were E2F and MYC sites, factors that are known to regulate both BDPs and FOXM1.
source: Among TF binding sites in the F/R-BDP were E2F and MYC sites, factors that are known to regulate both BDPs and FOXM1 (Barger et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2018; Bolognese et al., 2006; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citations to prior literature.

claim: The F/R-BDP displays several known characteristics of BDPs.
source: Thus, the F/R-BDP displays several known characteristics of BDPs.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the results section based on the data presented.

claim: TCGA and CCLE data revealed a progressive increase in both FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression with increasing copy number.
source: These analyses revealed a progressive increase in both FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression with increasing copy number (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: FOXM1 and RHNO1 mRNA and protein expression correlated with copy number in a laboratory collection of cell lines.
source: We validated that FOXM1 and RHNO1 mRNA and protein expression correlated with copy number, using a laboratory collection of cell lines, including immortalized Fallopian tube epithelium (FTE) cells (a precursor cell type for HGSC) and HGSC cells (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Although the associations between copy number and expression were significant, they were not uniform, indicating that mechanisms besides copy number status regulate FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression in HGSC.
source: Although the associations were significant, they were not uniform, indicating that mechanisms besides copy number status regulate FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression in HGSC.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is an inference based on the data presented.

claim: RT-qPCR analyses of an independent set of primary EOC tissues, and a panel of ovarian surface epithelium (OSE), FTE, and HGSC cell lines, indicated that FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression is highly correlated.
source: Consistent with TCGA HGSC data (Figure 2A), reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) analyses of an independent set of primary EOC tissues, and a panel of ovarian surface epithelium (OSE), FTE, and HGSC cell lines, indicated that FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression is highly correlated (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of FT282 and OVCAR8 cells showed that FOXM1 and RHNO1 showed significant co-expression in each case.
source: Next, to determine if this correlation occurs at the level of individual cells, we conducted single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of an immortalized human FTE cell line (FT282-C11, hereafter referred to as FT282) and a HGSC cell line (OVCAR8) (Barger et al., 2018; Domcke et al., 2013). Importantly, FOXM1 and RHNO1 showed significant co-expression in each case (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Both FOXM1 and RHNO1 showed elevated expression in OVCAR8 vs. FT282 cells, consistent with overexpression in cancer.
source: Both genes showed elevated expression in OVCAR8 vs. FT282 cells, consistent with overexpression in cancer (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4E.

claim: The FOXM1/RHNO1 correlation ranked in the top 1% of all BDG in FT282 and in the top 9% in OVCAR8 cells.
source: We next examined the degree of correlation seen between FOXM1 and RHNO1 as compared to other BDG genome-wide and, notably, observed that the FOXM1/RHNO1 correlation ranked in the top 1% of all BDG in FT282 and in the top 9% in OVCAR8 cells (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5.

claim: The high correlation between FOXM1 and RHNO1 supports a highly concordant regulatory process between FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression.
source: This observation supports a highly concordant regulatory process between FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is an inference based on the data presented.

claim: FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression correlates in biological contexts unrelated to ovarian cancer or its progenitor cells.
source: To address whether FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression correlates in biological contexts unrelated to ovarian cancer or its progenitor cells, we analyzed in silico gene expression data sets, including normal and cancer tissues and cells, and mouse and human data. Importantly, all comparisons revealed a highly significant correlation between FOXM1 and RHNO1, indicating that co-expression is a defining feature of this BDG unit (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Supplementary file 1.

claim: Co-expression is a defining feature of the FOXM1/RHNO1 BDG unit.
source: To address whether FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression correlates in biological contexts unrelated to ovarian cancer or its progenitor cells, we analyzed in silico gene expression data sets, including normal and cancer tissues and cells, and mouse and human data. Importantly, all comparisons revealed a highly significant correlation between FOXM1 and RHNO1, indicating that co-expression is a defining feature of this BDG unit (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Supplementary file 1.

claim: Both FOXM1 and RHNO1 were overexpressed in each category of cancer samples (primary tumors, metastatic tumors, and recurrent tumors) as compared to normal tissues.
source: Both FOXM1 and RHNO1 were overexpressed in each category of cancer samples (primary tumors, metastatic tumors, and recurrent tumors) as compared to normal tissues (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: FOXM1 showed greater overexpression in tumor tissues compared to RHNO1.
source: Moreover, FOXM1 showed greater overexpression in tumor tissues compared to RHNO1, and, consistently, the FOXM1/RHNO1 expression ratio was elevated in cancer (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6C.

claim: The FOXM1/RHNO1 expression ratio was elevated in cancer.
source: Moreover, FOXM1 showed greater overexpression in tumor tissues compared to RHNO1, and, consistently, the FOXM1/RHNO1 expression ratio was elevated in cancer (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6C.

claim: The elevated FOXM1/RHNO1 expression ratio in tumors was in part driven by relatively higher RHNO1 expression in normal tissues.
source: This was in part driven by relatively higher RHNO1 expression in normal tissues (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6B.

claim: After normalization to the canonical cell proliferation marker MKI67, the FOXM1/RHNO1 expression ratio was similar in normal and cancer tissues.
source: In agreement, after normalization to the canonical cell proliferation marker MKI67 (Whitfield et al., 2006), the FOXM1/RHNO1 expression ratio was similar in normal and cancer tissues (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6C.

claim: Increased FOXM1/RHNO1 expression in tumors might reflect increased cell proliferation as FOXM1 expression is closely associated with cell proliferation.
source: In addition, we hypothesized that increased FOXM1/RHNO1 expression in tumors might reflect increased cell proliferation as FOXM1 expression is closely associated with cell proliferation (Ye et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the results section and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Comparison of TCGA HGSC vs. GTEx Fallopian tube RNA-seq data revealed that both FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression show relatively uniform and highly significant increases in HGSC vs. Fallopian tube.
source: Comparison of TCGA HGSC vs. GTEx Fallopian tube RNA-seq data revealed that both FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression show relatively uniform and highly significant increases in HGSC vs. Fallopian tube (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7A.

claim: FOXM1 and RHNO1 were both significantly elevated in HGSC cell lines as compared to primary or immortalized FTE/OSE cells.
source: In agreement, FOXM1 and RHNO1 were both significantly elevated in HGSC cell lines as compared to primary or immortalized FTE/OSE cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7B.

claim: FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression significantly correlated in both primary and recurrent HGSC samples in two independent patient cohorts.
source: We compared FOXM1 vs. RHNO1 expression in primary and recurrent HGSC samples using two independent patient cohorts (Patch et al., 2015; Kreuzinger et al., 2017). In both cohorts, FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression significantly correlated in both primary and recurrent disease (Figure 8A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8A and 8B.

claim: 5/11 patients displayed coordinated upregulation of both FOXM1 and RHNO1 at recurrence.
source: While, overall, FOXM1 and RHNO1 expression wa﻿s not significantly altered in primary vs. recurrent disease, 5/11 patients displayed coordinated upregulation of both FOXM1 and RHNO1 at recurrence (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8C.

claim: FOXM1 and RHNO1 might contribute to disease recurrence in a large subset of HGSC patients.
source: This observation suggests that FOXM1 and RHNO1 might contribute to disease recurrence in a large subset of HGSC patients.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the results section based on the data presented.

claim: 5′ RNA ligase-mediated rapid amplification of cDNA ends (RLM-RACE) revealed TSSs consistent with NCBI Genome Browser data, revealing an intergenic span (i.e., between the 5′ ends of FOXM1 and RHNO1) of approximately 150 bp.
source: Initially, we determined the TSS of FOXM1 and RHNO1 in FTE (FT282) and HGSC (OVCAR4, OVCAR8) cells using 5′ RNA ligase-mediated rapid amplification of cDNA ends (RLM-RACE). The data revealed TSSs consistent with NCBI Genome Browser data, revealing an intergenic span (i.e., between the 5′ ends of FOXM1 and RHNO1) of approximately 150 bp (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The TSS of FOXM1 and RHNO1 are consistent between normal vs. HGSC cells.
